name: Progress Monitoring and Fidelity
title: Progress Monitoring and Fidelity
answer: Progress monitoring and fidelity is the practice of tracking, often weekly, whether a student is moving toward their goals and whether the planned intervention is actually being delivered. AI tools in spreadsheets and special education data systems can chart this data and write short summaries, which saves teacher time and makes patterns easier to spot. The tool never decides what the pattern means, because only the people who know the student can explain it.

sections.body: Progress monitoring is the ongoing collection of data on whether a student is moving toward their goals, usually done weekly so that teachers can watch for trends rather than wait for a single checkpoint. Fidelity is the related question of whether the intervention was delivered the way it was planned. The problem this idea solves is that both kinds of tracking take time and are easy to let slide, and busy teams may not notice a pattern until it is well established. AI tools inside spreadsheets and special education data systems can turn the collected data into charts and brief summaries, which reduces the workload and makes trends more visible. The point is not to replace judgment but to make the raw information easier for a team to use.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school or classroom, teachers collect progress data on a regular schedule, often weekly, and enter it into the spreadsheet or special education data system they already use. The AI features of those tools then produce charts and short written summaries of the trend. Teams use those summaries as the starting point for their meetings about a student, checking whether the intervention is being delivered as planned and whether the student is responding. The text does not give separate grade band examples, so the practice applies across ages in the same basic shape: gather the data, let the tool display it, then have the people who know the student read it. This keeps the routine light enough to sustain week after week.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this evidence as coming from a small review, which found that AI tools were associated with better monitoring of whether interventions were delivered as planned, a quality called fidelity (Mosher, 2026). The review included only five studies, so the links to student outcomes were indirect. The finding suggests that AI can help teams see whether services are actually happening. It does not yet show that students learn more as a result. The book is explicit that the outcome claim remains unproven.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The team interprets the data, not the tool. A summary might state that a student is not making progress, but the reasons could range from an ineffective intervention to missed sessions to a hard stretch at home, and only people who know the student can sort out which one it is. The data starts the conversation and the team finishes it, so the decision about what to change stays with the people, never with the software. The limits are also practical: the evidence base is small, and better fidelity monitoring is not the same as better learning. This description is about practice, not legal advice.
